author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Class 6 student what the smallest whole number is and you will often hear ‘one’. It is an honest slip, and it is exactly the confusion that class 6 maths whole numbers — NCERT Chapter 2 — is built to clear up. The smallest whole number is 0, not 1, and that single extra number changes how the whole set behaves. Once a child sees why 0 earns its place, the rest of the chapter — the number line, successors, predecessors, and the properties — falls into line quickly.

I have taught this chapter to plenty of Tier-2 city students who arrive thinking it is ‘too easy’ and leave realising the properties are the real prize. They are the rules that make mental arithmetic fast for the next six years. Here is how the chapter fits together.

Natural numbers vs whole numbers

Natural numbers are the counting numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, and so on. You use them to count real things — five mangoes, twelve students. But counting has no way to say ‘none’. Add the number 0 to the front of that list and you get the whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4…

So every natural number is a whole number, but 0 is the one whole number that is not a natural number. That is the entire difference — one number — and it is worth making a child say it out loud.

  • Natural numbers start at 1.
  • Whole numbers start at 0.
  • There is no largest whole number — you can always add one more.
  • 0 has no predecessor in the whole numbers (you cannot go one step below it here).

The number line

Draw a line, mark a point 0, and step off equal gaps to the right: 1, 2, 3, 4. That is the number line, and it turns arithmetic into movement. Addition is a jump to the right; subtraction is a jump to the left. To work out 3 + 4, you stand on 3 and take four steps right, landing on 7. For 6 − 2, you stand on 6 and take two steps left, landing on 4.

Multiplication is just repeated jumps of equal size: 3 × 4 means three hops of four, ending at 12. NCERT introduces the number line early precisely because it makes these operations visible rather than mysterious.

Successor and predecessor

The successor of a number is the one that comes just after it — add 1. The predecessor is the one just before — subtract 1. The successor of 24 is 25; the predecessor of 24 is 23. Every whole number has a successor, but only 0 has no predecessor among the whole numbers, which is a neat way to remember where the set begins.

The five properties (and why they save time)

This is the part that matters most. Five properties govern how whole numbers behave under addition and multiplication, and a student who truly owns them can shortcut sums that others do the long way.

PropertyWhat it saysExample
ClosureAdd or multiply two whole numbers, get a whole number7 + 5 = 12; 7 × 5 = 35
CommutativeOrder does not change the answer8 + 3 = 3 + 8; 8 × 3 = 3 × 8
AssociativeGrouping does not change the answer(2 + 3) + 4 = 2 + (3 + 4)
DistributiveMultiply a sum by splitting it6 × 12 = 6 × (10 + 2) = 60 + 12 = 72
Identity0 keeps addition unchanged; 1 keeps multiplication unchanged9 + 0 = 9; 9 × 1 = 9

Here is the counter-intuitive bit students miss: whole numbers are not closed under subtraction or division. Try 3 − 7 and you leave the whole numbers entirely — there is no whole-number answer. That gap is exactly why Class 6 later introduces integers and fractions.

Why the properties make mental maths easier

The distributive property alone is worth the whole chapter. Asked for 25 × 16, a student who knows it thinks 25 × (4 × 4) = (25 × 4) × 4 = 100 × 4 = 400 — no long multiplication. Commutativity lets you reorder 2 × 17 × 5 into (2 × 5) × 17 = 10 × 17 = 170. These are not tricks; they are the properties doing their job.

Case study 1: seats in the school auditorium

Read the passage, then solve. Vidaara Public School has an auditorium with 18 rows. Each row has 24 seats. For the annual day, 3 seats in each row are reserved for teachers.

  • Total seats? 18 × 24. Split it: 18 × (20 + 4) = 360 + 72 = 432 seats (distributive property).
  • Reserved seats? 3 in each of 18 rows = 18 × 3 = 54.
  • Seats left for students? 432 − 54 = 378.

Notice we used the distributive property to avoid long multiplication, then closure told us every result stayed a whole number — which makes sense, since you cannot have half a seat.

Case study 2: the tea-stall accounts

Ramesh sells 15 cups of tea before noon and 15 after. Each cup costs ₹10. What did he earn?

The slow way is 15 × 10 twice. The fast way uses two properties together: (15 + 15) × 10 by the distributive property is 30 × 10 = ₹300. If instead he sold 10 cups at ₹15, commutativity guarantees 10 × 15 gives the same ₹150 as 15 × 10 — the order of the factors never changes the takings. Real accounts are just the properties at work.

quiz.about: NCERT Class 6 Maths Chapter 2, Whole Numbers

questions.q: What is the smallest whole number?
questions.explanation: Whole numbers begin at 0. That is the one number that separates them from the natural numbers, which start at 1.

questions.q: Which number is a whole number but NOT a natural number?
questions.explanation: 0 is the only whole number that is not a natural number. Every other whole number is also natural.
The successor is one more than the number: 199 + 1 = 200.
The predecessor is one less than the number: 100 − 1 = 99.
Changing the order of the numbers without changing the answer is the commutative property.

questions.q: Whole numbers are NOT closed under which operation?
questions.explanation: 3 − 7 has no whole-number answer, so whole numbers are not closed under subtraction.
1 is the multiplicative identity: multiplying any whole number by 1 leaves it unchanged, so 46 × 1 = 46.

faq.q: Is 0 a whole number or a natural number?
faq.a: 0 is a whole number but not a natural number. Natural numbers start at 1, while whole numbers include 0 as well — that single number is the whole difference between the two sets.

faq.q: What are the five properties of whole numbers in Class 6?
faq.a: Closure, commutative, associative, distributive and identity. They describe how whole numbers behave under addition and multiplication, and they are the shortcuts behind fast mental arithmetic.

faq.q: Are whole numbers closed under subtraction and division?
faq.a: No. Subtraction like 3 − 7 and division like 5 ÷ 2 do not always give a whole-number answer. That gap is exactly why Class 6 later introduces integers and fractions.

faq.q: What is the difference between successor and predecessor?
faq.a: The successor is the number just after (add 1); the predecessor is the number just before (subtract 1). Every whole number has a successor, but 0 has no predecessor among the whole numbers.
